screens.title: Resolving Application and Service Problems
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn a practical, structured approach to get services and applications back into a healthy state. We'll focus on the commands and observations that reveal why a service failed, how to inspect the systemd unit and the journal for explanations, and how to identify runaway or unresponsive processes using process tools. You will also learn safe interventions: when to request a graceful stop, when force is required, and how to avoid causing data loss. Throughout, I will draw on concrete examples: using systemctl to view a service's state, reading unit-specific journal entries, using ps and top to find resource hogs, and applying kill or systemctl restart carefully. This is not just a checklist; it teaches the reasoning that links symptoms to root causes—permissions, missing files, dependencies, or kernel-level waits. By the end, you'll be able to triage a failing unit, gather the right logs, apply an informed fix, and clean up safely. Keep an eye out for common missteps, like assuming an active service is healthy or using kill -9 as a first response.

Resolving Application and Service Problems

A practical lesson in finding why services fail and how to restore them safely. You will learn to gather evidence, interpret process states, and choose the right remediation so services return to a reliable state.

Explore Key Topics
Service Diagnosis
Using systemctl and journalctl to find root causes and error messages.
Process Management
ps, top, and kill to locate unresponsive or resource-heavy processes.
Deep Diagnostics
When to use strace and lsof to see system calls and opened files.
Visual Concept
Process ↔ Service ↔ Logs
Process
Running programs, resource usage, signals.
Service
Systemd units, dependencies, and status codes.
Logs
Journal entries show errors, missing files, and permission problems.
Starter Tip

Always check journalctl for detailed explanations before making changes that can cause downtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to perform four concrete troubleshooting tasks. First, you will monitor and manage running processes using ps, top, and kill so you can find and control misbehaving programs. Second, you will inspect the status and logs of systemd services with systemctl and journalctl to discover startup errors and runtime faults. Third, you will identify common root causes such as missing dependencies, permission errors, and process states, and apply targeted fixes that resolve the underlying problem. Fourth, you will use diagnostic utilities like strace and lsof for deeper investigation when surface logs are insufficient. Each objective is practical: you will practice commands, interpret output, and understand when to prefer graceful shutdowns over forceful termination. These skills matter because a correct diagnosis reduces downtime, prevents data loss, and leads to repeatable fixes across servers. We'll also highlight common misconceptions, like assuming an active service is healthy or using kill -9 as a routine step.

screens.title: Process States and What They Mean
screens.narratorSegment: Process state indicators are small but powerful signals that guide diagnosis. When you read ps or top you'll see single-letter states: R for running, S for sleeping, D for uninterruptible sleep, Z for zombie, and T for stopped. Each state implies a different class of problem. A process in R is actively using C P U and likely doing work; if it consumes excessive C P U but should be idle, that points to a runaway loop. Sleeping processes commonly wait for events and are often harmless. A process in D is stuck waiting for input and output—this can be a disk or kernel-level block and suggests hardware or driver issues rather than application logic. Many Z processes indicate the parent isn't reaping children and point to a poorly written supervising program. Stopped processes are intentionally paused and may be awaiting a debugger or job control signal. A common misconception is to treat every high-C P U process as 'bad' without understanding its role; some services legitimately spike C P U during batch jobs. A quick example: a web server worker in D suggests it is blocked on file or device input and output, so check disks and mounts before restarting. Key takeaway: use state as a hypothesis generator for where to look next—logs, input and output stats, or parent processes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Process States
State Definitions
R — Running
Actively using CPU. Check what the process is doing before deciding it is misbehaving.
S — Sleeping
Waiting for an event. Often normal; inspect if causing blocking dependencies.
D — Uninterruptible Sleep
Usually waiting for I/O. Suggests disk, NFS, or kernel-level issues to investigate.
Analogy

Think of states as traffic lights: R is moving traffic, S is waiting at a signal, D is a stalled vehicle that needs mechanical attention.

Misconceptions & Remedies
  • Don't immediately kill a D-state process; investigate I/O and mounted filesystems first.
  • Multiple zombies suggest a parent process bug; restarting the parent may help, but verify consequences.
  • High CPU for batch jobs may be expected; check job schedules and maintenance windows.
Key Takeaway

Process state informs your next diagnostic step: check logs, I/O, or parent behavior accordingly.

screens.title: Finding and Observing Processes with ps and top
screens.narratorSegment: Two fundamental tools let you find the processes to investigate. ps aux gives a static snapshot that shows every user process with PID, C P U, memory, and command. Use options like --sort=-%C P U to find the highest C P U consumers. A concrete example: running ps aux --sort=-%C P U will list the busiest processes first so you can see which PID to inspect further. top provides a dynamic, updating view where you can watch C P U and memory use change in real time and interact to sort by different columns. A common pitfall is relying only on ps snapshots; a transient spike can be missed. Conversely, top can hide full command lines depending on terminal width, so combine both tools. After you find a suspicious PID, note its owner and parent PID; this matters for permission decisions and whether a parent can be restarted safely. Use ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd -p to see state and parentage. Remember to interpret output: the STAT column shows the process state shorthand we discussed earlier. This combined approach gives the evidence you need before attempting termination or deeper tracing.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ps & top
ps Example
'>ps aux --sort=-%cpu
Use the output to find the PID and user responsible for high CPU.
Quick Command
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd -p <PID> to inspect a single process with parent and state.
top Guidance
Run top to monitor processes as they change. Note PROCESS STAT and %CPU over several seconds before deciding to kill.
Example check

Misconception

A short snapshot may miss spikes; combine ps and top for full context.

screens.title: Safely Stopping Processes: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
screens.narratorSegment: Stopping a misbehaving process requires judgment. The default kill command sends SIGTERM, a polite request to shut down. SIGTERM gives the process a chance to perform cleanup, flush files, and release resources. Only when SIGTERM fails should you escalate to SIGKILL, which immediately terminates without cleanup. A concrete example: if a background worker is stuck trying to close a database connection, SIGTERM allows it to close connections gracefully. If it ignores signals or is in an uninterruptible D state, SIGKILL may have no effect or may cause orphaned resources. A common mistake is to use kill -9 as first choice; this can lead to data corruption, partially written files, or stale locks. Before using SIGKILL, verify the process owner and parentage, and consider service-level stops (systemctl stop) when the process is managed by systemd. If you must use SIGKILL, be aware you may need to restart dependent services and check journals for subsequent errors. Key takeaway: prefer graceful termination, escalate only when necessary, and always check for side effects afterward. Safely Stopping Processes: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL means send sigterm to allow cleanup; escalate to sigkill only when the process is unresponsive and the risk of leaving it running outweighs cleanup risks.. In practical terms, when to ask politely and when to forcefully terminate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
Orderly Shutdown (SIGTERM)
'>kill <PID>  # sends SIGTERM (15)
Allows the process to save state and release resources.
Forceful Termination (SIGKILL)
'>kill -9 <PID>  # sends SIGKILL (9)
Immediate stop; no cleanup. Use only when necessary.
Decision Flow
Try kill, wait and confirm the process exits. If it remains, examine state (D means likely I/O) and parent. Only use -9 when unresponsive and you understand the trade-offs.

screens.title: Using systemctl to Inspect and Control Services
screens.narratorSegment: systemctl is the primary way to manage services under systemd and is often the first tool in a service troubleshooting flow. Running systemctl status with a service name returns the unit state—active, inactive, failed—along with recent log entries and the service's main PID if available. This output often includes a short hint about why a service failed. For example, systemctl status apache2 may show 'failed' and list an exit code and a brief message. But status is only the starting point: inspect dependencies and unit relationships—After= and Wants=—when services fail due to ordering or missing prerequisites. A common mistake is relying on status alone. Always follow with journalctl -u to see detailed unit logs. When restarting, use systemctl restart to let systemd manage dependencies and ordering, and consider systemctl daemon-reload only after editing unit files. If the service is masked or disabled, you will need to unmask or enable it before starting. Treat systemctl commands as service-aware operations that preserve unit semantics rather than killing processes directly when units are managed by systemd. Using systemctl to Inspect and Control Services means use systemctl for start/stop/restart so systemd enforces unit dependencies and restarts.. In practical terms, reading status, unit relationships, and recent failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › systemctl
Typical Commands
Check status
'>systemctl status <service_name>
Restart safely
'>systemctl restart <service_name>
Note: systemctl manages ordering and restarts according to unit configuration. Avoid killing a process that is managed by systemd without considering the unit semantics.
Hint

If a service is masked, systemctl will prevent it from starting; unmask before starting.

Misconception

Don't conflate a running process with a healthy unit; check unit logs and health checks where applicable.

screens.title: Using journalctl to Read Unit-Specific Logs
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl provides the detailed log entries you need after systemctl shows a failure. Use journalctl -u -xe to filter by unit, jump to the end, and include explanatory text when available. The -x option often adds helpful context or suggested actions to some messages. When diagnosing, set a time window such as --since '5 minutes ago' to isolate recent failures. Read entries for permission denied errors, missing file errors, or library load failures. These messages will frequently point to the missing path or configuration file that caused the unit to exit. A common mistake is to rely on system logs in /var/log alone; systemd centralizes messages in the journal and may contain kernel-level errors or unit-specific diagnostics that traditional logs miss. If you see repeated restart attempts in the journal, the Restart= behavior in the unit may mask the root cause; inspect the unit file and the journal together. Example: a No such file or directory error for ExecStart indicates the binary or script path is wrong. Combine journal output with file checks and permission listing to form a corrective action plan.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › journalctl
Common Patterns
Use these journalctl invocations to narrow your search and read explanation text when available.
'>journalctl -u <service_name> -xe
journalctl -u <service_name> --since '5 minutes ago'
Reading Clues
  • Look for 'No such file or directory' to find missing binaries or scripts.
  • Permission denied errors point to incorrect service user rights.
  • Repeated crash loops reveal configuration or dependency problems.
Example
If journalctl shows a missing ExecStart script, confirm the path with ls -l and ensure the service's User has execute permission. Fix the path or create the script and restart the service.

screens.title: Missing Dependencies and Permission Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Many service failures boil down to missing dependencies or permission problems. A missing library (. so) or a required helper service not starting will prevent a unit from functioning. Similarly, a service user without the correct read or write permissions on configuration or data directories will see permission denied entries in the journal. Diagnosis starts with reading journalctl for messages about missing libraries or 'permission denied'. Then validate the filesystem: ls -l on the relevant files and directories will show ownership and mode bits. Check which user the service runs as in the unit file and confirm that user has the needed access. For dependencies, examine the unit's After= and Wants= directives and ensure those units are active. A practical example: a web server that cannot read /var/www/html due to incorrect ownership will log permission denied. Fix ownership with chown and set correct permissions before restarting. A common misconception is to over-broaden permissions (for example chmod 777) — instead prefer minimal privileges required. Always document changes and back up configuration files before editing them. Missing Dependencies and Permission Errors means confirm the service user and file ownership; fix with targeted chown/chmod rather than permissive changes.. In practical terms, why services fail on startup and how to validate prerequisites. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Dependencies & Permissions
Common Checks
  • Look for 'No such file' or shared-library errors in journal entries.
  • Check file ownership: ls -l /path/to/file or directory.
  • Verify the service's User in its unit file and confirm permissions.
Practical Fix
Use chown to set the correct owner and chmod to adjust access. Avoid 777; prefer minimal rights necessary for operation.
'>ls -l /var/www/html
chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
chmod -R 750 /var/www/html
Reminder
Always back up config files before changing ownership or permissions, and test in a safe environment when possible.

screens.title: When to Use strace and lsof
screens.narratorSegment: If logs and service status don't reveal the cause, strace and lsof can expose what a process is actually doing. strace traces system calls and signals and shows operations like open, read, write, connect, and their errors. Attaching strace to a PID can reveal attempts to open missing files or failing network connections. For example, strace -p will show which system calls return errors, which is especially helpful when a process repeatedly tries and fails to access a resource. lsof lists all open files and network sockets for a process and helps you see which files, libraries, or sockets are in use. Running lsof -p will show the file descriptors and paths that the process has opened. These tools are powerful but can produce a large volume of output; filter and capture relevant lines, and run them in a controlled environment. A common mistake is to run strace on a busy production process without understanding the performance impact. Use these tools for targeted, time-limited inspection and always document findings so changes can be reviewed. When to Use strace and lsof means use strace to see failing system calls and lsof to list open resources when logs are insufficient.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Dealing with Runaway or Unresponsive Applications
screens.narratorSegment: Runaway processes can render a system unresponsive, and the response must balance urgency with safety. Start by confirming the impact: are other services affected, is swap thrashing occurring, or is input and output saturated? Use ps aux --sort=-%mem or --sort=-%C P U and top to confirm the culprit and its PID. If possible, notify users and schedule a short maintenance window for production systems. Attempt a graceful shutdown first with kill; if the process ignores SIGTERM, verify its state—if it's in D, the kernel is waiting for input and output and kill may not work. If the system is unusable and the process cannot be stopped, kill -9 may be required, but expect potential data inconsistency. After termination, inspect related logs and open files with lsof to detect leftover locks or partial writes. In clustered services, follow cluster-aware procedures such as fencing or failover rather than killing a node process. Finally, adjust limits or scheduling to prevent recurrence: use ulimit, cgroups, or tune application settings. The key is to contain impact, gather evidence, and apply a measured fix that prevents repeated outages.

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulating a Failed systemd Service
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the lab scenario step by step. First, create a simple unit file with an ExecStart pointing to a non-existent script to simulate failure. Finally, clean up by stopping and disabling the unit and removing the files you created, followed by daemon-reload. screens.title: Safe Restart and Cleanup Procedures
screens.narratorSegment: When you repair a service, follow a safe restart and cleanup process. First, record the current state and collect logs so you can audit changes later. Use systemctl stop to halt services managed by systemd and wait for them to exit gracefully. After applying configuration or file fixes, use systemctl daemon-reload if you edited unit files and then systemctl restart to let systemd apply unit ordering and restart dependencies. Verify service health with status and journalctl, and run a smoke test such as an HTTP request for a web service or a connection check for a database. When removing temporary artifacts from a debug session, stop and disable the unit if it won't be used, remove files you created, and run systemctl daemon-reload. In production, prefer rolling restarts or maintenance windows; never run these cleanup steps on a critical node without coordination. A common oversight is failing to check for orphaned files or locks after forceful termination—confirm with lsof and application logs. Key takeaway: a careful restart and cleanup reduces risk of repeated outages and data corruption. In this chapter you will learn a practical, structured approach to get services and applications back into a healthy state. We'll focus on the commands and observations that reveal why a service failed, how to inspect the systemd unit and the journal for explanations, and how to identify runaway or unresponsive processes using process tools. You will also learn safe interventions: when to request a graceful stop, when force is required, and how to avoid causing data loss. Throughout, I will draw on concrete examples: using systemctl to view a service's state, reading unit-specific journal entries, using ps and top to find resource hogs, and applying kill or systemctl restart carefully. This is not just a checklist; it teaches the reasoning that links symptoms to root causes—permissions, missing files, dependencies, or kernel-level waits. By the end, you'll be able to triage a failing unit, gather the right logs, apply an informed fix, and clean up safely. Keep an eye out for common missteps, like assuming an active service is healthy or using kill -9 as a first response.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to perform four concrete troubleshooting tasks. First, you will monitor and manage running processes using ps, top, and kill so you can find and control misbehaving programs. Second, you will inspect the status and logs of systemd services with systemctl and journalctl to discover startup errors and runtime faults. Third, you will identify common root causes such as missing dependencies, permission errors, and process states, and apply targeted fixes that resolve the underlying problem. Fourth, you will use diagnostic utilities like strace and lsof for deeper investigation when surface logs are insufficient. Each objective is practical: you will practice commands, interpret output, and understand when to prefer graceful shutdowns over forceful termination. These skills matter because a correct diagnosis reduces downtime, prevents data loss, and leads to repeatable fixes across servers. We'll also highlight common misconceptions, like assuming an active service is healthy or using kill -9 as a routine step.

This lesson includes hands-on tasks designed to build confidence. You'll create a dummy failing systemd unit and practice the full loop: detect failure, read the unit status, inspect journal entries, and apply a minimal fix. You'll also practice finding a resource-hungry process with ps and top, attempt a graceful termination, and escalate to a forceful kill if needed. For advanced debugging, you'll run strace to watch system calls and use lsof to list open files and sockets. Each practice item teaches a judgment: when to restart a service, when to edit permissions or configuration, and when to coordinate downtime. These activities are low-risk when performed on a lab VM and emphasize safety: back up configs, avoid blind commands found online, and schedule changes during maintenance when in production. Completing these tasks helps you translate logs and process states into concrete remediation steps.

Process state indicators are small but powerful signals that guide diagnosis. When you read ps or top you'll see single-letter states: R for running, S for sleeping, D for uninterruptible sleep, Z for zombie, and T for stopped. Each state implies a different class of problem. A process in R is actively using C P U and likely doing work; if it consumes excessive C P U but should be idle, that points to a runaway loop. Sleeping processes commonly wait for events and are often harmless. A process in D is stuck waiting for input and output—this can be a disk or kernel-level block and suggests hardware or driver issues rather than application logic. Many Z processes indicate the parent isn't reaping children and point to a poorly written supervising program. Stopped processes are intentionally paused and may be awaiting a debugger or job control signal. A common misconception is to treat every high-C P U process as 'bad' without understanding its role; some services legitimately spike C P U during batch jobs. A quick example: a web server worker in D suggests it is blocked on file or device input and output, so check disks and mounts before restarting. Key takeaway: use state as a hypothesis generator for where to look next—logs, input and output stats, or parent processes.

Two fundamental tools let you find the processes to investigate. ps aux gives a static snapshot that shows every user process with PID, C P U, memory, and command. Use options like --sort=-%C P U to find the highest C P U consumers. A concrete example: running ps aux --sort=-%C P U will list the busiest processes first so you can see which PID to inspect further. top provides a dynamic, updating view where you can watch C P U and memory use change in real time and interact to sort by different columns. A common pitfall is relying only on ps snapshots; a transient spike can be missed. Conversely, top can hide full command lines depending on terminal width, so combine both tools. After you find a suspicious PID, note its owner and parent PID; this matters for permission decisions and whether a parent can be restarted safely. Use ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd -p to see state and parentage. Remember to interpret output: the STAT column shows the process state shorthand we discussed earlier. This combined approach gives the evidence you need before attempting termination or deeper tracing.

Stopping a misbehaving process requires judgment. The default kill command sends SIGTERM, a polite request to shut down. SIGTERM gives the process a chance to perform cleanup, flush files, and release resources. Only when SIGTERM fails should you escalate to SIGKILL, which immediately terminates without cleanup. A concrete example: if a background worker is stuck trying to close a database connection, SIGTERM allows it to close connections gracefully. If it ignores signals or is in an uninterruptible D state, SIGKILL may have no effect or may cause orphaned resources. A common mistake is to use kill -9 as first choice; this can lead to data corruption, partially written files, or stale locks. Before using SIGKILL, verify the process owner and parentage, and consider service-level stops (systemctl stop) when the process is managed by systemd. If you must use SIGKILL, be aware you may need to restart dependent services and check journals for subsequent errors. Key takeaway: prefer graceful termination, escalate only when necessary, and always check for side effects afterward. Safely Stopping Processes: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL means send sigterm to allow cleanup; escalate to sigkill only when the process is unresponsive and the risk of leaving it running outweighs cleanup risks.. systemctl is the primary way to manage services under systemd and is often the first tool in a service troubleshooting flow. Running systemctl status with a service name returns the unit state—active, inactive, failed—along with recent log entries and the service's main PID if available.
